lead: A hollow metal pipe a few centimetres across carries microwave power with very little loss. It cannot carry a plain wave like a coaxial cable: the field must fit the metal walls, so only certain patterns — modes — survive, and each mode has a cutoff frequency below which it dies away. The pipe dimensions and two integers called mode indices set that cutoff, the guide wavelength and the wave velocities. Waveguides feed horn antennas and form the bench hardware of every microwave laboratory.
prereq: You need: the propagation constant, phase velocity and wavelength of 1.1, plus basic electromagnetics (Maxwell's equations and the boundary condition on a conductor).

sections.h3: Why a hollow pipe has modes

blocks.text: Inside a hollow metal guide a wave cannot have any pattern it likes: the tangential electric field must vanish on a perfect conductor, so the field across the guide is pinned at the walls and settles into a standing-wave pattern, like a rope fixed at both ends.

Only patterns that fit exactly survive. Two integers label each one: m counts half-cycles of field variation along the broad wall a (metres), n along the narrow wall b (metres). That gives two families:

items: TE modes (transverse electric): Ez = 0, Hz ≠ 0 — no electric field along the guide axis.
TM modes (transverse magnetic): Hz = 0, Ez ≠ 0 — no magnetic field along the axis.
TEM is impossible: it needs two separate conductors, as in a coaxial cable, not one hollow pipe.

blocks.text: Every mode has a cutoff frequency fc. Below fc the fields decay exponentially along the guide and carry no real power: the mode is evanescent. Above fc it propagates. So a waveguide is a high-pass device for each mode, with no upper limit.

For TE10 the electric field runs across the guide parallel to the narrow wall, strongest at the centre of the broad wall and zero at its side walls. Wall current density is Js = n̂ × H, so current lines cross the magnetic field lines at right angles. At the centre of the broad wall the TE10 current runs only along the guide, so a slot cut lengthwise there cuts no current: that is why slotted measuring lines work.

sections.h3: Rectangular guide: cutoff, guide wavelength, velocities

blocks.text: For a guide of broad wall a and narrow wall b filled with a dielectric of relative permittivity εr, the cutoff frequency of the TEmn or TMmn mode is:

blocks.where: c = 3×10⁸ m/s; a, b in metres; m, n the mode indices; εr = 1 for air filling. TM modes need m ≥ 1 and n ≥ 1.

blocks.text: The cutoff wavelength follows directly, and the wavelength actually measured inside the guide is longer than in free space:

blocks.where: λc, λg, λ0 in metres; λ0 = c/(f√εr) at operating frequency f in hertz.

blocks.text: Two velocities describe the wave. Phase velocity vp is the speed of a point of constant phase; group velocity vg is the speed of the energy and of the modulation:

blocks.where: vp, vg in m/s. Near cutoff vp is far above c and vg near zero; far above cutoff both approach c/√εr.
η = 377/√εr Ω is the filling's intrinsic impedance; ηTE is above η, ηTM below.

blocks.text: The lowest cutoff belongs to TE10: fc10 = c/(2a√εr). It is the dominant mode. Next come TE20 at c/(a√εr) and TE01 at c/(2b√εr); choosing b < a/2 keeps TE01 above TE20 and gives a single-mode band from fc10 to 2fc10. TE11 and TM11 share a higher cutoff, (c/(2√εr))·√(1/a² + 1/b²); TM modes need m ≥ 1 and n ≥ 1. Above the single-mode band several modes travel at different velocities and the signal smears.
A circular guide of radius a (metres) uses cylindrical field patterns and Bessel functions in place of sines. Its cutoff is set by a Bessel root:

blocks.where: p is the Bessel root for the chosen TEnm or TMnm mode, from the table; a in metres; c = 3×10⁸ m/s.

blocks.text: TE11 is dominant, but two polarisations share its cutoff, so a slight bend or ovality makes the pattern rotate. Circular guide is used where the joint must turn, as in rotating radar joints and dish feeds, and its TE01 mode has wall loss that falls as frequency rises, which suits long runs. Rectangular guide stays the bench default: clean mode spacing and polarisation fixed by the walls.

examples.question: An air-filled rectangular waveguide has a = 2.286 cm and b = 1.016 cm. (a) Find the cutoff frequencies of TE10, TE20 and TE01 and the single-mode band. (b) At 10 GHz find λg, vp, vg and the wave impedance of TE10. Take c = 3×10⁸ m/s and η = 377 Ω.
steps: a = 0.02286 m, b = 0.01016 m; air filling, so εr = 1.
Order 6.56 < 13.12 < 14.76 GHz, so the single-mode band is 6.56 to 13.12 GHz.
10 GHz lies in the single-mode band, so only TE10 propagates.
examples.answer: fc10 = 6.56 GHz, fc20 = 13.12 GHz, fc01 = 14.76 GHz, single-mode band 6.56 to 13.12 GHz; at 10 GHz λg = 3.98 cm, vp = 3.98×10⁸ m/s, vg = 2.26×10⁸ m/s and ZTE = 500 Ω.
examples.check:
c = 3e8
a = 2.286e-2
b = 1.016e-2
f = 10e9
fc10 = c / (2*a)
fc20 = c / a
fc01 = c / (2*b)
print(round(fc10/1e9, 2))
print(round(fc20/1e9, 2))
print(round(fc01/1e9, 2))
lam0 = c / f
root = (1 - (fc10/f)**2)**0.5
print(round(lam0/root*100, 2))
print(round(377/root))

examples.question: The same guide is driven at 18 GHz. Which modes propagate? Find λg, vp, vg and the wave impedance of TE20 and TM11.
steps: Cutoffs from fc = (c/2)√((m/a)² + (n/b)²): TE10 6.56, TE20 13.12, TE01 14.76, TE11 and TM11 16.16, TE30 19.69, TE21 and TM21 19.75 GHz.
Every mode with fc < 18 GHz travels: TE10, TE20, TE01, TE11 and TM11, five modes. λ0 = c/f = 1.667 cm.
Check: vp·vg = 4.38×10⁸ × 2.05×10⁸ = 8.98×10¹⁶ ≈ c² for TE20, and 6.80×10⁸ × 1.32×10⁸ = 8.98×10¹⁶ for TM11. The mode nearer its cutoff has the longer λg and the slower energy.
examples.answer: Five modes propagate. TE20: λg = 2.44 cm, vp = 4.38×10⁸ m/s, vg = 2.05×10⁸ m/s, Z = 551 Ω. TM11: λg = 3.78 cm, vp = 6.80×10⁸ m/s, vg = 1.32×10⁸ m/s, Z = 166 Ω.

traps: Using λ0 where λg is needed. Phase shift along a guide is 2π per λg, not per λ0, so a guide section is longer than the free-space path for the same shift.
Saying a mode 'does not exist' below cutoff. It is evanescent: the field decays as e<sup>−αz</sup> and carries no real power.
Writing a TM mode with m = 0 or n = 0. Ez ∝ sin(mπx/a)·sin(nπy/b) vanishes if either index is zero, so TM11 is the lowest TM mode.
Swapping a and b. The broad wall a sets fc10; using b is wrong by more than a factor of two for standard X-band guide.
Forgetting √εr. A filling of εr = 4 halves every fc and changes λ0 to c/(f√εr).

quiz.q: Define TE and TM modes in a waveguide and state which field component is zero in each.
quiz.a: TE (transverse electric): Ez = 0, Hz ≠ 0. TM (transverse magnetic): Hz = 0, Ez ≠ 0. Each mode keeps the fields transverse to the direction of propagation plus one axial component.

quiz.q: Why can a hollow rectangular waveguide not support a TEM mode?
quiz.a: TEM needs a transverse field derived from a potential that is constant on each conductor. A hollow pipe is one conductor, so the potential is the same everywhere on its wall, Laplace's equation then makes it constant inside, and the field is zero. TEM needs two separate conductors, as in coax.

quiz.q: For the guide of the worked example (a = 2.286 cm, b = 1.016 cm, air filled), find the cutoff frequency of the TE11 mode.
A circular air-filled waveguide has radius 1 cm. Find the cutoff frequency of its dominant mode. Take the Bessel root for TE11 as 1.841 and c = 3×10⁸ m/s.
quiz.a: fc = p·c/(2πa) = 1.841 × 3×10⁸/(2π × 0.01) = 8.79×10⁹ Hz = 8.79 GHz. TE11 is dominant because 1.841 is the smallest root.

quiz.q: A guide is used at a frequency just 2% above fc10. Give two practical problems that follow from the formulas for vp, vg and wave impedance.
quiz.a: √(1 − (1/1.02)²) = 0.197. λg ≈ 5.1λ0 and changes fast with frequency, so the phase of a guide run swings strongly with small frequency or dimension errors (strong dispersion). vg ≈ 0.2c, so the group delay is five times the free-space value and pulses spread. ZTE ≈ 377/0.197 ≈ 1910 Ω, hard to match to a probe, and wall loss rises steeply near cutoff. That is why this guide is used only from about 1.25fc to 1.9fc (8.2 to 12.4 GHz).

beyond: Not for the exam. Satellite payloads still use rectangular guide for its low loss, and substrate-integrated waveguide (SIW) builds the same guide from two rows of plated vias in a printed board, so these cutoff and λg formulas carry over. Search 'substrate-integrated waveguide' and 'waveguide mode chart'.
